scope: 16 existing taxa, 17 display profiles; original reconstruction, not an independent scientific certification.

species.corrections: Fuller fusiform trunk, moderately arched mouth and small rounded flippers. Retained two shallow throat creases, small posterior fin, and no right-whale callosities.
species.physiology: Baleen filters small plankton, including copepods and krill documented in stomach contents. Detailed live feeding mechanics remain poorly observed; a right-whale-like feeding animation would overstate the evidence.

species.corrections: Deeper thorax and shorter taper, narrow arched rostrum with one principal ridge, tall hooked posterior fin, 42 short ventral grooves and sparse irregular oval scars.
species.physiology: Baleen retains small prey after water is filtered. Sei whales use both skim feeding and engulfment, with copepods, krill and small schooling fish in their diet. Their ventral grooves are relatively short compared with many rorquals.

species.corrections: Pointed rostrum, fuller chest, modelled shoulder contour, discrete white pectoral bands and a pale ventrum with lateral shoulder shading. Retained 56 ventral grooves.
species.physiology: Engulfment of schooling fish and small crustaceans uses a distensible ventral pouch followed by baleen filtration. This northern phenotype has a white mid-flipper band; the band is not a feeding organ or universal to every common-minke form.

species.corrections: Fuller Antarctic-minke body, pointed rostrum, darker unbanded pectorals, pale underside and 30 ventral grooves. This is a separate phenotype from the northern common minke.
species.physiology: Engulfment and baleen filtration capture Antarctic krill and other prey. The selected 30-groove field is within NOAA’s 22–38 range. This animal lacks the northern common-minke mid-flipper band; baleen colour can be asymmetric.

species.corrections: Fuller trunk and caudal peduncle, three rostral ridges, bilateral pale ventrum and revised hooked fin. No false Omura-type jaw asymmetry.
species.physiology: Rice’s whales are baleen filter feeders. Limited tag records indicate deep daytime foraging near the seafloor and shallower nighttime occupancy. These observations do not justify a universal surface-lunge trajectory or a species-wide dive schedule.

species.corrections: Fuller Bryde/Eden body and revised fins, three rostral ridges and 48 ventral grooves. Both existing display profiles remain; neither authored shape diagnoses the contested species split.
species.physiology: Bryde/Eden whales filter small schooling fish and crustaceans through baleen after taking in prey and water. The archive retains two display forms under one disputed taxon concept; morphology and this single mitochondrial record do not resolve the proposed split.

species.corrections: One rostral ridge, right pale lower jaw and blaze, asymmetric flank chevrons and pale pectoral leading edges. Revised thorax, hooked fin and 86 long ventral grooves.
species.physiology: Observed Madagascar animals performed lunge feeding. Small crustaceans were found in the study area, but complete prey composition was unresolved. The asymmetric jaw, blaze and chevrons are identification features; a pale jaw does not imply a different filtration mechanism.

species.corrections: Rounded adult melon, robust trunk, deepened caudal peduncle, broad anterior dorsal fin and long swept flippers. Selected ventral anchor and subtle saddle remain individual artwork.
species.physiology: Long-finned pilot whales hunt squid and also consume fish. Echolocation supports prey finding in dark water. Teeth assist prey capture, while suction can contribute to ingestion; no generic rorqual pouch or baleen belongs on this odontocete.

species.corrections: Rounded beakless melon with median crease, robust thorax, narrow tailstock, tall falcate dorsal fin and tapered pectorals. Pale head and grouped, curved rake scars replace uniform random scratches.
species.physiology: Risso’s dolphins primarily take squid and other cephalopods. The sparse anterior mandibular teeth, usually two to seven pairs with no upper teeth, differ from a dolphin’s full conical tooth rows. Some studied adults initiated deep foraging dives with a right-sided roll.

species.corrections: Long narrow rostrum with revised jawline, fuller flexible trunk, broad rounded flippers, small eyes and low long dorsal ridge. Selected gray-pink mottling is not a universal adult colour.
species.physiology: Botos capture a variety of fish with a long rostrum. Anterior teeth are conical, while posterior teeth have flanges that assist processing prey. Mobile cervical anatomy and broad flippers aid manoeuvring; pinkness varies with age, sex and individual history.

species.corrections: Long beak and smoothly rising melon, fuller but slender trunk, upright dorsal fin, swept pectorals and a three-part Gray’s spinner pigment pattern. No fish-like lateral tail sweep.
species.physiology: Spinner dolphins feed mainly at night on mesopelagic fish, squid and shrimp. In Hawaiian populations, daytime resting and nighttime offshore feeding are well documented; that local routine is not assumed for every population. Aerial spins are a separate behaviour from underwater propulsion.

species.corrections: Rounded melon, moderate beak, fuller trunk, curved dorsal fin, lateral blaze and distinct eye-to-flipper and eye-to-anal pigment branches. Stripes are separate from the mouth crease.
species.physiology: Striped dolphins feed on fish and cephalopods, with prey and dive patterns varying geographically. Echolocation helps detect prey. Their characteristic eye-to-flipper and eye-to-anal stripes are pigment paths, not anatomical seams or grooves.

species.corrections: Rounded beakless forehead, short mouthline, fuller trunk, broad rounded flippers, small posterior fin and a forward-opening U-shaped blowhole slit. No Australian snubfin range is inferred.
species.physiology: Irrawaddy dolphins consume fish and other prey in coastal, estuarine and some river habitats. Broad flippers support manoeuvring and the rounded head lacks a projecting beak. This archive record excludes the separately recognised Australian snubfin dolphin.

species.corrections: Rounded overhanging forehead of the selected mature male, short bottle-shaped rostrum, robust trunk, small posterior fin and short pectorals. Apical teeth are hidden in this closed-mouth model.
species.physiology: Northern bottlenose whales are deep-diving odontocetes that primarily take squid, with other prey also recorded. Suction feeding suits the short rostrum and reduced dentition. The apical teeth of adult males are generally hidden with the mouth closed.

species.corrections: Low sloping melon, raised male mandibular arch, forward-angled erupted teeth behind the tip, fuller midbody and small posterior fin. Body marks remain selected individual artwork.
species.physiology: Blainville’s beaked whales forage at depth on squid and fish. Reduced dentition and suction feeding differ from a dolphin’s tooth-lined grasping jaws. The selected mature male has erupted teeth on the raised lower jaw behind the tip; females and juveniles differ.

species.corrections: Compact, deep body with a sloping blunt head, short underslung mouth, small flippers and a relatively tall central dorsal fin. The false-gill crescent follows the eye region and is only pigment.
species.physiology: Dwarf sperm whales take squid and other prey using suction-assisted feeding. Their underslung lower jaw bears most teeth. The pale false-gill crescent is skin pigment; the animal breathes air through a blowhole and has no gills. Defensive reddish fluid is released from the intestine.
